summary.text: Wilson’s theorem determines the square of the half-factorial; when it is a square root of 1, a quadratic-character reindexing turns the matrix into an odd-column mixture of commuting skew-symmetric and symmetric matrices, whose determinant vanishes (the commutation follows from an inversion substitution in a finite-field character sum). When the half-factorial squares to 1, Euler’s criterion converts the matrix modulo p to a power matrix, and a binomial moment argument together with two Vandermonde matrices and the polynomial \(\prod_{j=1}^m(X-j)\) shows that any kernel vector has all moments, hence all entries, zero.

full_proof.text:
Let \(n\ge 2\), let \(p=p_n\) be the \(n\)-th prime, and put
\[
 m=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
Since \(n\ge2\), we have \(p>2\), so \(p\) is odd and
\[
 p=2m+1.
\]
Write \(\mathbb F_p=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\), and let
\[
 \chi:\mathbb F_p\longrightarrow\{-1,0,1\}
\]
be the quadratic character, with \(\chi(0)=0\). For an integer argument, the Legendre symbol modulo \(p\) is exactly this character applied to its residue class. Set
\[
 a_i=i\in\mathbb F_p\qquad(1\le i\le m),
 \qquad \varepsilon=m!\in\mathbb F_p.
\]
Thus the matrix whose determinant defines \(a(n)\) is
\[
 M=(M_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le m},\qquad
 M_{ij}=\chi(a_i^2-\varepsilon a_j).
\]
We prove that \(\det M=0\) exactly when \(p\equiv3\pmod4\).

We first record several elementary facts that will be used in both directions.

### 1. Representatives and the half-factorial

The elements \(a_1,\dots,a_m\) are nonzero and pairwise distinct. Moreover, no two of them are negatives of one another: if \(a_i+a_j=0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), then \(p\mid i+j\), whereas
\(2\le i+j\le2m=p-1\), which is impossible. It follows in particular that their squares are pairwise distinct. Indeed, \(a_i^2=a_j^2\) implies \(a_i=a_j\) or \(a_i=-a_j\), and the second alternative is impossible.

Every nonzero element of \(\mathbb F_p\) is uniquely one of
\[
 a_1,\dots,a_m,-a_1,\dots,-a_m.
\]
Consequently, for every function \(F\) on \(\mathbb F_p\), with values in any additive commutative group,
\[
 \sum_{u\in\mathbb F_p^\times}F(u^2)
 =2\sum_{i=1}^m F(a_i^2).                                      \tag{1}
\]

Wilson's theorem gives a useful formula for \(\varepsilon\). Pair the factors in
\((p-1)!=(2m)!\) into the first half \(1,\dots,m\) and the second half \(m+1,\dots,2m\). Modulo \(p=2m+1\), the latter half is, in reverse order, \(-1,-2,\dots,-m\). Hence
\[
 (p-1)!\equiv (-1)^m(m!)^2\pmod p.
\]
Since Wilson's theorem says \((p-1)!\equiv-1\), we obtain
\[
 \boxed{\ \varepsilon^2=(-1)^{m+1}\ }.                         \tag{2}
\]

We will also use the following standard properties of the quadratic character:
\[
 \chi(xy)=\chi(x)\chi(y),
 \qquad \chi(y^2)=1\quad(y\ne0),                                \tag{3}
\]
and
\[
 \chi(-1)=
 \begin{cases}
  1,&p\equiv1\pmod4,\\
 -1,&p\equiv3\pmod4.
 \end{cases}                                                     \tag{4}
\]

### 2. A mixed-column determinant lemma

We need a general linear-algebraic observation. Suppose \(A\) and \(B\) are square matrices over a characteristic-zero integral domain, indexed by a finite set, and suppose
\[
 A^T=-A,\qquad B^T=B,\qquad AB=BA.                               \tag{5}
\]
Given a subset \(S\) of the column indices, form a matrix \(C_S\) by taking column \(j\) from \(A\) when \(j\in S\), and from \(B\) when \(j\notin S\). Then
\[
 |S|\text{ odd}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \det C_S=0.           \tag{6}
\]

Here is a proof. First suppose \(B\) is invertible, and put
\[
 R=B^{-1}A.
\]
The commutation relation implies that \(B^{-1}\) commutes with \(A\). Therefore, using (5),
\[
 R^T=A^T(B^{-1})^T=(-A)B^{-1}=-B^{-1}A=-R;

the matrix \(R\) is skew-symmetric. Also \(A=BR\). Thus
\[
 C_S=BN,
\]
where column \(j\) of \(N\) is column \(j\) of \(R\) for \(j\in S\), and column \(j\) of the identity for \(j\notin S\).

By elementary column elimination, the entries of the selected columns in rows outside \(S\) can be removed using the identity columns indexed outside \(S\). More explicitly, if \(N'\) agrees with \(N\) except that
\[
 N'_{ij}=0\quad\text{when }i\notin S,
 \ j\in S,
\]
then \(N=N'(I+E)\) for a matrix \(E\) supported in rows outside \(S\) and columns inside \(S\). The precise determinant of \(I+E\) is immaterial, because \(N'\) already has determinant zero. After ordering indices so that those in \(S\) come first, \(N'\) is block diagonal with the principal block \(R[S,S]\) and an identity block. The principal block remains skew-symmetric and has odd size. Every odd-dimensional skew-symmetric matrix over a domain of characteristic different from two has determinant zero: if its size is \(r\), then
\[
 \det R[S,S]=\det R[S,S]^T=\det(-R[S,S])=(-1)^r\det R[S,S]
 =-\det R[S,S],
\]
so twice its determinant is zero. This proves (6) when \(B\) is invertible.

For general \(B\), introduce an indeterminate \(t\) and replace \(B\) by
\[
 B_t=B+tI.
\]
This matrix is still symmetric and commutes with \(A\). Its determinant is a monic polynomial in \(t\), and hence is nonzero. It is therefore invertible over the fraction field of the polynomial ring. The preceding argument shows that the mixed-column determinant formed from \(A\) and \(B_t\) is zero in that fraction field, and hence is the zero polynomial. Evaluating at \(t=0\) yields (6) for the original pair \(A,B\).

### 3. A character-sum identity

For nonzero \(x,z\in\mathbb F_p\), we claim
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{l=1}^m
 \chi\bigl((x^2-a_l^2)(a_l^2+z^2)\bigr)\\
 &\hspace{25mm}=
 \sum_{l=1}^m
 \chi\bigl((x^2+a_l^2)(a_l^2-z^2)\bigr).                       \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]

By (1), twice the left side is the corresponding sum over all
\(u\in\mathbb F_p^\times\), and similarly on the right. In the all-units sum on the left, make the bijective substitution
\[
 u\longmapsto \frac{xz}{u}.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\left(x^2-\left(\frac{xz}{u}\right)^2\right)
 \left(\left(\frac{xz}{u}\right)^2+z^2\right)\\
 &\qquad=\left(\frac{xz}{u^2}\right)^2
 (x^2+u^2)(u^2-z^2).
\end{aligned}
\]
The prefactor is the square of a nonzero element, so its character is \(1\). Thus the two all-units sums are equal. Equation (1) then says that twice the two sides of (7) are equal as integers, and cancellation of \(2\) proves (7).

## The case \(p\equiv3\pmod4\)

Suppose now that \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). Then \(m\) is odd and \(\chi(-1)=-1\). From (2),
\[
 \varepsilon^2=1,

the field has odd characteristic, and therefore
\[
 \varepsilon=1\quad\text{or}\quad\varepsilon=-1.               \tag{8}
\]
It follows from \(\chi(-1)=-1\) that, after regarding \(\chi(\varepsilon)\in\{\pm1\}\) as an element of \(\mathbb F_p\),
\[
 \chi(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon,                                 \tag{9}
\]
and of course \(\chi(\varepsilon)^2=1\).

For each \(j\), consider
\[
 q_j=\chi(a_j)a_j\in\mathbb F_p.
\]
This is a nonzero square. If \(\chi(a_j)=1\), this follows directly from the characterization of nonzero squares by the quadratic character. If \(\chi(a_j)=-1\), then
\[
 \chi(q_j)=\chi(-a_j)=\chi(-1)\chi(a_j)=(-1)(-1)=1.
\]
Thus there is an index \(\sigma(j)\in\{1,\dots,m\}\) such that
\[
 a_{\sigma(j)}^2=q_j=\chi(a_j)a_j.                               \tag{10}
\]
The map \(\sigma\) is injective. Indeed, equality of the right sides of (10) for \(j\) and \(j'\) says either \(a_j=a_{j'}\), when the two character signs agree, or \(a_j=-a_{j'}\), when they disagree. The latter is impossible by the representative facts above, and the former gives \(j=j'\). Since the set is finite, \(\sigma\) is a permutation.

Define two integer matrices
\[
 (\Phi_-)_{ik}=\chi(a_i^2-a_k^2),
 \qquad
 (\Phi_+)_{ik}=\chi(a_i^2+a_k^2).                                \tag{11}
\]
The first is skew-symmetric: exchanging \(i,k\) multiplies the argument by \(-1\), whose character is \(-1\). The second is symmetric. Moreover, they commute. Indeed,
\[
 (\Phi_-\Phi_+)_{ik}
 =\sum_{l=1}^m
 \chi\bigl((a_i^2-a_l^2)(a_l^2+a_k^2)\bigr),
\]
whereas
\[
 (\Phi_+\Phi_-)_{ik}
 =\sum_{l=1}^m
 \chi\bigl((a_i^2+a_l^2)(a_l^2-a_k^2)\bigr).
\]
These sums are equal by (7), with \(x=a_i\) and \(z=a_k\).

Partition the column indices by
\[
 S=\{j:\chi(\varepsilon)\chi(a_j)=1\}.                          \tag{12}
\]
We claim that \(|S|\) is odd. Every factor
\(\chi(\varepsilon)\chi(a_j)\) is either \(1\) or \(-1\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \prod_{j=1}^m\chi(\varepsilon)\chi(a_j)
 &=\chi(\varepsilon)^m\chi\left(\prod_{j=1}^m a_j\right)\\
 &=\chi(\varepsilon)^m\chi(\varepsilon)
 =\chi(\varepsilon)^{m+1}=1,                                   \tag{13}
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(\prod_j a_j=m!=\varepsilon\), \(m\) is odd, and
\(\chi(\varepsilon)^2=1\). Hence the number of factors equal to \(-1\), namely \(m-|S|\), is even. Since \(m\) is odd, \(|S|\) is odd.

Now permute the columns of \(M\) by \(\sigma\). Formula (10) shows how each resulting column is expressed in terms of (11). If \(j\in S\), then
\(\chi(a_j)=\chi(\varepsilon)\); using (9),
\[
 a_{\sigma(j)}^2=\chi(a_j)a_j=\varepsilon a_j,

the \(j\)-th column of \(M\) is therefore the
\(\sigma(j)\)-th column of \(\Phi_-\). If \(j\notin S\), then
\(\chi(a_j)=-\chi(\varepsilon)\), so
\[
 a_{\sigma(j)}^2=-\varepsilon a_j,

the \(j\)-th column of \(M\) is the
\(\sigma(j)\)-th column of \(\Phi_+\). Thus, up to a column permutation, \(M\) is obtained by choosing the columns indexed by the permuted set \(S\) from \(\Phi_-\), and the remaining columns from \(\Phi_+\). The set still has odd cardinality. Since \(\Phi_-\) is skew-symmetric, \(\Phi_+\) is symmetric, and the two matrices commute, the mixed-column lemma gives
\[
 \det M=0.                                                       \tag{14}
\]

## The case \(p\equiv1\pmod4\)

Suppose instead that \(p\equiv1\pmod4\). Then \(m\) is even. Formula (2) now gives
\[
 \varepsilon^2=-1.                                              \tag{15}
\]
In particular \(\varepsilon\ne0\).

We prove that \(\det M\ne0\). Assume for contradiction that the integer determinant is zero. Reduce the matrix modulo \(p\). Euler's criterion, including the case of a zero argument, says
\[
 \chi(x)\equiv x^{(p-1)/2}=x^m\pmod p.                           \tag{16}
\]
Consequently the matrix over \(\mathbb F_p\)
\[
 K_{ij}=(a_i^2-\varepsilon a_j)^m                               \tag{17}
\]
has determinant zero. There is therefore a nonzero vector
\(v=(v_1,\dots,v_m)^T\in\mathbb F_p^m\) with \(Kv=0\).

For \(r\ge0\), define its moments
\[
 \mu_r=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j^r v_j.                                  \tag{18}
\]
Expanding every row equation of \(Kv=0\) by the binomial theorem gives, for every \(i\),
\[
 0=\sum_{k=0}^m (a_i^2)^k c_k,                                  \tag{19}
\]
where
\[
 c_k=\binom{m}{k}(-\varepsilon)^{m-k}\mu_{m-k}.                 \tag{20}
\]
The \(m\) elements \(a_i^2\) are pairwise distinct. Furthermore Fermat's theorem gives
\[
 (a_i^2)^m=a_i^{2m}=a_i^{p-1}=1.                                \tag{21}
\]
Thus all \(a_i^2\) are roots of \(T^m-1\), and, being \(m\) distinct elements, they are exactly its roots.

Let \(F(T)=\sum_{k=0}^m c_kT^k\). By (19), \(F\) vanishes at these same \(m\) distinct points. Subtracting \(c_m(T^m-1)\) from \(F\) produces a polynomial of degree at most \(m-1\) which still vanishes at all \(m\) points. It must therefore be zero. Comparing coefficients gives
\[
 c_k=0\quad(1\le k<m),
 \qquad c_0+c_m=0.                                               \tag{22}
\]
This is equivalently the invertibility of the Vandermonde matrix on the distinct numbers \(a_i^2\).

For \(0<r<m\), take \(k=m-r\) in the first part of (22). The factors
\((-\varepsilon)^r\) are nonzero. Also \(\binom mr\) is nonzero modulo \(p\). To see the latter, if \(p\mid\binom mr\), then from
\[
 \binom mr r!(m-r)!=m!
\]
we would get \(p\mid m!\), impossible because \(m<p\). Hence (20) implies
\[
 \mu_r=0\qquad(0<r<m).                                          \tag{23}
\]
The endpoint relation in (22), using \(c_0=(-\varepsilon)^m\mu_m\) and \(c_m=\mu_0\), is
\[
 (-\varepsilon)^m\mu_m+\mu_0=0.                                \tag{24}
\]

We need one more relation between \(\mu_m\) and \(\mu_0\). Consider
\[
 g(T)=\prod_{j=1}^m(T-a_j).
\]
This is monic of degree \(m\), and, because \(m\) is even,
\[
 g(0)=\prod_{j=1}^m(-a_j)=(-1)^m m!=\varepsilon.                 \tag{25}
\]
Write \(g(T)=\sum_{r=0}^m g_rT^r\). Thus \(g_0=\varepsilon\) and \(g_m=1\). Since \(g(a_j)=0\) for every \(j\),
\[
 0=\sum_{j=1}^m v_jg(a_j)
   =\sum_{r=0}^m g_r\mu_r.
\]
All intermediate terms vanish by (23), so
\[
 \varepsilon\mu_0+\mu_m=0,
 \qquad\text{or}\qquad
 \mu_m=-\varepsilon\mu_0.                                      \tag{26}
\]
Because \(m\) is even, \((-\varepsilon)^m=\varepsilon^m\). Substitution of (26) into (24) yields
\[
 \mu_0\bigl(1-\varepsilon^{m+1}\bigr)=0.                       \tag{27}
\]
We claim that \(\varepsilon^{m+1}\ne1\). If it were \(1\), then its square would also be \(1\), whereas (15) and the oddness of \(m+1\) give
\[
 (\varepsilon^{m+1})^2=(\varepsilon^2)^{m+1}
 =(-1)^{m+1}=-1.
\]
This is impossible in \(\mathbb F_p\), since \(p\) is odd and hence \(1\ne-1\). Therefore (27) implies
\[
 \mu_0=0.
\]
Together with (23), this says
\[
 \mu_r=0\qquad(0\le r<m).                                      \tag{28}
\]

But (28) is the homogeneous Vandermonde system
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^m a_j^rv_j=0\qquad(0\le r<m).
\]
Its coefficient matrix has determinant
\(\prod_{i<j}(a_j-a_i)\), which is nonzero because the \(a_j\) are pairwise distinct. Hence \(v=0\), contradicting the choice of a nonzero kernel vector. This contradiction proves
\[
 \det M\ne0\qquad\text{when }p\equiv1\pmod4.                   \tag{29}
\]

Finally, every odd prime is congruent to either \(1\) or \(3\pmod4\). Equation (14) handles the second case, and (29) handles the first. Since the Jacobi symbols in the definition are Legendre symbols for the prime modulus \(p=p_n\), the determinant in that definition is precisely \(\det M\). Therefore, for every \(n\ge2\),
\[
 \boxed{\ a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_n\equiv3\pmod4\ }.
\]
